title: Paul tells his story (Acts 22)
hookLine: arrested, he asks to speak and tells of Damascus in Hebrew
tomorrow: men swear not to eat until Paul is dead. who overhears?
last: THE WILL OF THE LORD BE DONE.

cards: Job interviews, college essays, first dates: sooner or later someone says, so, tell me about yourself. Paul gets that question in a setting nobody would choose.
Roman soldiers have just pulled him out of a crowd at the temple and are carrying him up the steps of the castle, as the King James calls their fortress.

Halfway up, he asks the commander one thing: let me speak to the people. He turns, raises his hand, and when they hear him speak in the Hebrew tongue, Acts says "they kept the more silence." And he tells them a story.

teach.h: WHO HE WAS: AT GAMALIEL'S FEET.
teach.b: He doesn't open with an argument. He opens with who he is: "I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel."
He admits the worst part plainly: he once hunted down people who followed this way. Then the road to Damascus, about noon.
"Suddenly there shone from heaven a great light round about me." He falls, and hears a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?"
He answers, "Who art thou, Lord?" and the reply comes: "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest." Then his second question, the one today's line comes from: "What shall I do, Lord?" Not why me.
Not prove it. What shall I do.

He's led by the hand into Damascus, unable to see, and a devout man named Ananias stands by him and says, "Brother Saul, receive thy sight." That's the whole shape: who he was, what happened, who helped, what he asked.
One to tell a friend tonight: the turning point of the story is a question. The crowd listens until he says he's been sent to the Gentiles, and the shouting starts again.
So what does this give you for the next time someone says, tell me about yourself?
Name who helped. Leave the polish out.

how: Some Christians share a testimony, the plain story of how faith came into their lives, in church, in small groups, or with friends.

games.q: what does “paul tells his story” mean?
o: Paul's own account of the Damascus road
a letter Paul wrote to Jerusalem's leaders
a sermon on the law delivered in Athens

p: Paul was brought up at his feet
about noon, on the Damascus road

s: Paul's speech on the stairs is a clever legal argument
it's his own story, told plainly: who he was, what happened, who helped.
Paul told the crowd he had once persecuted this way
he admits it plainly, before he tells of the light.
Paul addressed the crowd in Latin, the language of Rome
Acts says he spoke in the Hebrew tongue, and they kept the more silence.

games.q: at your grandma's memorial, you're asked with no warning to say a few words. what would Paul's speech on the stairs suggest?
o: say plainly who she was, what happened, and who helped her.
read a well-known poem so you don't have to say anything yourself.
politely decline; a eulogy needs time and a polished version.
games.why: Paul had no notes and a hostile crowd. he told it plainly: who he was, what happened, who helped, what he asked.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write your own story in three short lines: who I was, what happened, what I'm asking now. Keep it plain; nobody will read it but you. If you pray, you can end with Paul's question: what shall I do, Lord?

wordCard.voice: Paul tells his story. On the castle stairs, in the Hebrew tongue: who he was, what happened, who helped, and what he asked.

orig.note: Greek: Saul, the form of his name the voice uses in Acts 22:7.

carryVoice: Your line: what shall I do, Lord? It was Paul's second question, and the one that changed his road. See you tomorrow.
